beats.narration_text: Guten Tag. This is Liam, in for Bear. Anthropic's claude code security review won't catch every security bug. It reads one pull request at a time, and only what changed. So the real question is the risks this change adds.

beats.narration_text: A pull request: a proposed change, waiting for review before it's merged. The diff: just the lines a change adds or removes. And a false positive: a flagged problem that isn't real.

beats.narration_text: Here's a pull request: a crate on a belt, on its way to being merged. The security review is a GitHub Action, a job GitHub runs when a pull request opens. It puts Claude over the belt, as a security reviewer.

beats.narration_text: Open the crate. Most of the repo stays behind. Only the changed files go under review. Claude can read the rest for context, but it's told to report only what this pull request adds, not old problems.

beats.narration_text: The changed files pass under the scanner. Claude reads them for meaning, not just patterns, looking for things like injection, broken authentication, exposed secrets and weak crypto. Each suspect becomes a finding: the line, how serious, how it could be exploited, and a fix.

shot.visual_intent: The three pages ride under the dark arch; a terracotta scan line sweeps each; white finding flags pop up on dark-kraft poles above two of them ('finding'); one flag opens into a finding card (a dark title bar and four grey lines: line, severity, exploit, fix).

beats.narration_text: Before anything is posted, a filter catches likely false positives. Hard rules drop low-impact kinds, like denial of service and rate limits. Then Claude re-checks each finding, and drops the ones it isn't confident in.

shot.visual_intent: Four finding flags ride toward a kraft-framed mesh screen ('filter'); the first flag hits the mesh and drops into a grey bin below; a second is checked by the arch's light and also drops ('dropped'); two pass through.

beats.narration_text: What's left lands on the pull request as review comments, pinned to the exact lines, each with a thumbs up and a thumbs down. The prompt puts it plainly: better to miss a theoretical issue than flood you with false positives.

beats.narration_text: Then a person decides. The action posts a comment review. It doesn't approve the pull request, and it doesn't merge it. You read each comment, fix what's real, and dismiss what isn't.

beats.narration_text: You can also run the same review yourself. Claude Code ships a slash command, slash security review, that reviews the pending changes on your branch. Copy it into your project, and you can tune it.

beats.narration_text: One caution, in the repo's own words: the action is not hardened against prompt injection. A pull request could carry text written to steer the reviewer. So run it only on trusted pull requests, and have a maintainer approve outside contributors before their workflows run.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude Code: Add Anthropic's claude code security review to this repo as a GitHub Action. Trigger it on pull requests only, read the API key from a repository secret, and exclude our vendored and generated folders. It must never run on untrusted pull requests, so tell me how to require approval for outside contributors. I'll treat its comments as leads to check, not verdicts. Then check two things yourself. Does the workflow run on pull requests only, with the key in a secret? And in your repo settings, do outside contributors need approval?
